ig_caption:
Myth: a rental loss always cuts the tax on your paycheck.
Fact: the IRS treats most rentals as passive, so the loss you can use against W-2 pay has a limit.

✔️ If you help run the rental (approve tenants, set rent, OK repairs), up to $25,000 of loss can offset other income.
✔️ That amount drops by 50 cents for each dollar of modified AGI over $100,000.
✔️ At $150,000 it's gone. The loss isn't lost; it carries forward.

Example: income of $130,000 and a $15,000 rental loss. $10,000 counts this year, $5,000 waits.

Before Dec 31, run your 2026 rental numbers so April has no surprises.

li_caption:
A rental that shows a loss on paper does not always lower the tax on a W-2 salary. Many owners learn this in April.

The IRS treats most rental real estate as a passive activity. Passive losses generally offset only passive income, with one important exception.

1. Owners who actively participate (at least 10% ownership and real decisions such as approving tenants, setting rent and approving repairs) can use up to $25,000 of rental loss against other income.
2. The $25,000 drops by 50% of modified AGI over $100,000 and is gone at $150,000. Married filing separately has lower limits.
3. Loss that can't be used is not lost. It carries forward to later years.
4. Real estate professionals who meet the 750-hour test follow different rules.

Example: modified AGI of $130,000 and a $15,000 rental loss. $10,000 offsets other income this year; $5,000 carries forward.

Before Dec 31, run the 2026 rental numbers so the return holds no surprises. We work with landlords and short-term rental hosts on exactly this.

sources.fact: Active participation: up to $25,000 of rental real estate loss against nonpassive income; reduced by 50% of MAGI over $100,000; generally none at $150,000+ ($12,500/$50,000/$75,000 MFS if lived apart all year; none if lived together); active participation = 10% by value + management decisions such as approving new tenants, setting rental terms, approving expenditures; disallowed loss carries over to the next year; real estate professionals >750 hours (Pub 925, 2025 edition, read 2026-11-17; IRC 469(i) amounts are fixed, not inflation-indexed)
$130,000 / $15,000 example is an illustration (25,000 - 50% x 30,000 = 10,000), not a client or statistic
